text:
## Direct answer

There is no "best card" I can name for you from here as a live pick — and any answer that hands you a ranked list of *currently tradable* cards has to come from the live catalog, not from memory. When I queried the card index, the cards that resolve (SpaceX IPO card `EVCDX-SPACEX-SETS-ASIDE-UP`, the "AI optimism" card `EVCDX-STOCKS-BOUNCE-AS-AI`) are **settled** — their trading windows closed 2026-06-04/05 and they finished at index 95.98 (−4.02%) and 96.55 (−3.45%) respectively. That is the key structural fact for a first trade: **news-driven event cards have a finite trading window and can and do close red.** So step one is enumerating what is actually open right now, then sizing conservatively because you have zero realized edge yet.

I verified there is **no grounded backtest return on the event-card pipeline** (the ontology returns `grounded_return: null` across all seven event-pipeline paths). That means I must not quote you an expected return for any card — none is measured. Treat all sizing below as risk control, not a profit forecast.

## 1. Which cards to trade first — the enumeration + selection path

Do not pick from a static list. Pull the live set and filter it:

- **List live cards:** `GET https://cymetica.com/api/v1/event-cards` (public, no auth). This is the authoritative active-card feed; the `/events` deck is the human view of the same data.
- **Inspect any candidate:** MCP `get_event_card_info(query=<title|EVCDX ticker|id>)` → returns the full basket + weights, `current_index` vs `index_base`, `pct_since_inception`, `status`, and `trading_closes_at`. Only trade cards whose `status` is active and whose `trading_closes_at` is comfortably in the future.

Rank the live set by these, in order:
1. **Status = active with runway** — reject anything near its `trading_closes_at`; you want time for the thesis to play out.
2. **Basket you can actually price and reason about** — prefer baskets whose legs are liquid crypto or large-cap equity you can independently value. Note the settled examples above were dominated by one name (the SpaceX card was ~72% PLTR): a "card" can be a concentrated single-name bet in disguise. Read the weights before trading.
3. **A basket you can backtest.** For crypto-leg baskets you can get evidence *before* committing: MCP `backtest_event_card_idea`. As a concrete calibration run, a 40/30/30 BTC/ETH/SOL basket over the last 90 days returned +33.77% with Sharpe 3.53, Sortino 7.59, max drawdown 10.13%, VaR₅ −2.61% (fees applied, 90 points). **That is a hypothetical buy-and-hold of an arbitrary basket, not a live card and not a promise** — I show it only so you have a real drawdown/volatility number (~10% peak-to-trough) to size against. Stock-leg cards can't be backtested this way (no daily history), so treat those as higher-uncertainty.
4. **Direction is a decision, not a default.** Each card trades UP (`direction=bull`) or DOWN (`direction=bear`). Pick the side your thesis supports; don't assume long.

If you want a card that doesn't exist yet, build one from a theme/URL (`create_event_card`, or the explicit-leg `build_custom_event_card` / `/events/builder`) — but that debits a one-time $0.99 creation fee and is unnecessary for a first paper trade when live cards already exist.

## 2. How to size the first position

You have an **unproven edge**, so use fractional-Kelly *or* a fixed risk budget — never full Kelly on trade one.

- **Kelly output (verified):** at a modest assumed edge (win prob 0.55, win/loss ratio 1.5), **quarter-Kelly on a 100,000 USDC bankroll = 6,250 USDC (6.25%)**, expected value +0.375 per dollar *at those assumptions*, capped below the 10% ceiling. If your assumed win probability is lower or unknown, this number should come down, not up.
- **Risk-budget cross-check (the one I'd anchor to for trade one):** risk **1% of bankroll = 1,000 USDC** of loss. Using the ~10% basket drawdown above as your stop distance, that implies a **~10,000 USDC notional** first position with a stop near −10%. If you set a tighter −5% stop, notional halves to ~5,000 USDC for the same 1% risk. This keeps you in the game across many independent card trades and lets you diversify into low-correlation cards (square-root-of-N Sharpe benefit) rather than concentrating.

Net: **first position ≈ 5,000–10,000 USDC (5–10% of the 100k), skewing to the lower end until the card book shows a realized edge.** Never exceed a 10% single-position cap on trade one.

## 3. Execution path (paper, no reply needed)

- Trade a card directly: MCP `trade_event_card(direction=bull|bull, ...)` — paper by default, costs nothing.
- Or via REST on the index token's book: `POST https://cymetica.com/api/v1/exchange/<EVCDX-SYMBOL>/orders` (EVCDX tokens: NAV ≈ $1.00, tick $0.0001, min order 1 EVCDX).
- To let a cloned bot trade cards automatically: `update_bot_settings(instance_id, event_card_trading_enabled=true)`.
- Read state before/after: `get_event_card_info` for index level; the card's page `https://cymetica.com/events/<id>`.

## Caveats
Past backtest figures are hypothetical and not indicative of future results; no event card carries a measured/grounded return, so I've quoted none. This is research tooling, not personalized financial advice, and models can be wrong — verify the live card list and each basket's weights before committing.

Here is the answer for the asking agent.

---

**Direct answer on the target first.** I can give you a concrete, tool-grounded paper-trading process on `trade_event_card`, but I cannot give you a plan that "turns 100,000 into 1,000,000." That is a 10× (+900%), and no honest plan promises it — reaching it would require concentrated, high-variance bets whose single most likely outcome is a large drawdown, not the target. Concretely: the strongest recent basket I backtested below returned +27.86% over 90 days (with fees); compounding 10× at that rate needs ~9.4 consecutive 90-day windows (~2.3 years) with *no* losing quarter — not a plannable path, just a tail outcome. So what follows is a disciplined process to deploy the 100k paper bankroll with positive expectancy and bounded risk. The target is a hope, not a plan; the process below is the plan.

**What I verified just now (evidence):** I probed open cards via `get_event_card_info` across SpaceX / AI / crypto / Bitcoin themes. Every card it surfaced is **settled** — trading already closed:
- `EVCDX-SPACEX-SETS-ASIDE-UP` (id 5b3d9a69…) — status **settled**, index 95.98 (−4.02%), closed 2026-06-04.
- `EVCDX-STOCKS-BOUNCE-AS-AI` (id 21792b73…) — **settled**, 96.55 (−3.45%), closed 2026-06-05.
- `EVCDX-CRYPTO-EXCHANGE-BINA` (id e555c61f…) — **settled**, 95.19 (−4.81%), closed 2026-06-04.
- `EVCDX-BITCOIN-S-TRAPPED-UN` (id a5c850b9…) — **settled**, 88.20 (−11.80%), closed 2026-06-01.

Today is 2026-09-10, so I cannot hand you a verified *currently-open* card to "open first" — the ones my lookups return are stale. **Do not trade any card without first confirming `status` is active and `trading_closes_at` is in the future.** That confirmation is step 1 below.

**The executable plan (all tools named exist on your MCP surface):**

1. **Build the open-card universe.** Browse the live deck at cymetica.com/events, and for any known card id fetch `GET /api/v1/event-cards/{id}`. For every candidate, call `get_event_card_info` and keep only those with `status` = active and a future `trading_closes_at`. This replaces guessing — I found zero confirmable-open cards, so you assemble the live set yourself here. Also use `search_markets` / `list_markets` for the broader market list.

2. **Pre-trade evidence, free and read-only.** For each candidate, run `backtest_event_card_idea` on its basket (crypto legs only; stock-heavy baskets like the SpaceX one return no daily history) over period_days 90 and 180. Keep only baskets with a positive return *and* Sharpe > ~1 *and* max-drawdown you can tolerate. Worked example I just ran — BTC 0.6 / ETH 0.3 / SOL 0.1, 90d, 100k, fees on: ending 127,857 USDC, **+27.86%**, Sharpe 3.55, Sortino 7.94, max drawdown 10.38%, VaR5 −2.50%. That is the bar a candidate should clear, not a forecast.

3. **Direction — you set it, from the basket, not from me.** `trade_event_card` takes `direction=bull` (trade up) or `bear` (trade down). Decide per card from its `pct_since_inception`, its basket composition, and your thesis on the underlying names. There is no default correct side; if you have no directional view on a card, skip it.

4. **Sizing — risk-based, not target-based.** Do not size to hit 1M. Risk a fixed fraction of the bankroll per position: **1.5–2% of 100k = 1,500–2,000 USDC of *risk* per card**, where risk = notional × stop distance. With an 8% stop, that is ~18,750–25,000 USDC notional per card. Cap concurrent exposure at **8–12 low-correlation cards** (different themes/baskets — not ten BTC-correlated cards; correlated positions are one bet in disguise) and total gross deployed ≤ ~60–70% of bankroll, keeping dry powder. Track fills and exposure with `get_positions` and `get_order_history`; check the book with `get_orderbook` and marks with `get_prices` before each entry.

**Close rule (every position gets all three, set at entry):**
- **Hard stop:** exit at −8% from entry index (caps loss to your ~2% risk budget).
- **Profit protection:** once +15%, trail the stop to lock gains rather than using a fixed take-profit — let winners run, cut losers fast.
- **Time exit (mandatory for cards):** be flat before `trading_closes_at` — cards settle, so never carry one into resolution expecting to manage it after close.
Re-evaluate the whole book daily against fresh `get_event_card_info` (index moved? basket rebalanced?) and re-backtest before re-entering.

**Why this and not a "10× blueprint":** positive-expectancy setups (step 2) + bounded per-trade risk (step 4) + asymmetric exits (close rule) is the only structure that survives a losing streak. It can compound the paper balance; it cannot and will not be promised to reach any specific number. Past backtest performance is not indicative of future results.

**Tools/endpoints referenced (all on your surface):** `get_event_card_info`, `backtest_event_card_idea`, `trade_event_card` (paper by default), `search_markets`, `list_markets`, `get_market`, `get_orderbook`, `get_prices`, `get_positions`, `get_order_history`; plus `GET /api/v1/event-cards/{id}` and the cymetica.com/events deck for the live-card universe.

text:
**No trade can be composed to *deliver* $1,000 → $1,200.** +20% is a target, not an outcome any instrument on this platform (or anywhere) can guarantee. Anyone who hands you a "compose a trade that turns X into 1.2X" answer as if the +20% is assured is fabricating. What I *can* do is compose real, executable setups whose historical evidence I can carry, and tell you exactly what each one needs to go right — and what it costs you if it doesn't. Every number below is a backtested/historical figure pulled live, not a projection.

## What +20% actually requires
A one-shot +20% is a large move. Your three honest levers are: (1) an unleveraged directional basket that has to rise ~20% on its own, (2) a strategy bot whose *backtest* cleared ~20%, or (3) leverage on a smaller move. Ranked, grounded candidates:

### Candidate A — Directional crypto basket (unleveraged, the cleanest risk)
I backtested a 60% BTC / 40% ETH buy-and-hold, $1,000, trailing 180 days, round-trip costs applied:
- **Total return: +8.06%** ($1,000 → $1,080.64) · Sharpe 0.87 · **max drawdown −30.6%** · Sortino 1.57.
- Read: over the last 6 months this basket did **not** reach +20%, and it drew down 30% along the way. To net +20% unleveraged you need a stronger up-move than the recent regime delivered. This is the lowest-mechanism-risk path but it did not clear your goal historically.
- Iterate/execute: re-test any basket with `backtest_event_card_idea` (change legs/weights/window); launch it as a tradeable card via `trade_event_card` (paper by default) or the builder at https://cymetica.com/events/builder. Live spot legs: `place_order` on the CLOB, or `GET /api/v1/clob`.

### Candidate B — A strategy whose backtest actually cleared ~20%
From the platform's grounded backtest index (real `backtest_results` rows, not estimates), the setups that historically hit your target:
- **Hybrid 2 (Blue)** — long-only RSI+MACD+ATR across stocks & crypto: **+19.86% total, Sharpe 2.79, max DD 1.75%, win-rate 27%, 177 trades** (run 2026-03-15). Closest single match to your +20% goal at low historical drawdown.
- **Hybrid 2 (Red)** — short side: +17.42%, Sharpe 2.81, max DD 3.68%.
- **StockBull (Blue)** — EMA 9/21 + RSI/MACD equities long: +17.02%, Sharpe 2.70, max DD 3.91%.
- Caveat that matters: these are single historical windows. A 27% win-rate carrying a +20% result means a few trades did the work — that is fragile out-of-sample. Treat it as evidence, not a forward number.
- Act on it: details at `GET /api/v1/ontology/master/encyclopedia/bt-hybrid2-blue`; resolve the exact instrument→venue→execution chain with `find_trade_path` (slug `bt-hybrid2-blue`); run your own backtest at `GET /api/v1/backtest`; clone/run the bot via `GET /api/v1/bots`. In the NEXUS chat on cymetica.com you can clone and fund this as a bot directly.

### Candidate C — Leverage (only if you accept liquidation risk)
On the native perp venue, a smaller underlying move reaches +20% with leverage — e.g. ~+7% on a 3x isolated long ≈ +20% on margin, before funding/fees. But the same leverage means a ~7% adverse move wipes the position's margin (isolated: only that collateral, not your whole $1,000). Live specs first: `GET /perp/markets/{symbol}` for mark, max leverage, funding; trade at https://cymetica.com/perp/trade/{symbol}. This is the fastest path to +20% and the fastest path to −100% of the stake. Highest risk of the three.

## Straight recommendation
If your real constraint is "highest chance of +20% for the least downside," none of these is a sure thing — but **Candidate B (Hybrid 2 Blue)** is the only path whose *own history* both reached ~20% and held drawdown under 2%, so it's where I'd point the evidence. Before committing real capital, re-run it over a fresh/out-of-sample window at `GET /api/v1/backtest` and size so a full loss is survivable. Candidate A is the honest "no leverage, no guarantees" option that recently returned ~8%, not 20%. Candidate C gets you to 20% on a smaller move but can zero the stake.

This is research, not financial advice, and backtests are historical — past results do not predict the next $1,000. Verify every figure yourself at the endpoints above before trading.

## Answer: clone **Perceptron Oracle**

**First, what "Hybrid 2 (Blue)" actually is.** It is not a clonable bot species at all — that is why it is absent from `GET /api/v1/cloned-bots/available`. In the grounded ontology it is `bt-hybrid2-blue`, a **backtest strategy configuration** (dimension `backtest_returns`, category `backtest_strategy`), defined as: *"Long-only mixed-asset bot combining RSI, MACD and ATR across both stocks and crypto — diversified upside, sourced from the top WTA market."* Its grounded backtest (`source: backtest_results`, `fabricated: false`, `run_id 73b31f87-8825-4e19-b103-5a93aa67ad21`, ran 2026-03-15T13:11:26Z) recorded: total return **+19.86%**, Sharpe **2.7787**, win rate **27.12%**, max drawdown **1.75%**, over **177 trades**. So the goal you are pursuing has three defining features: (1) **long / upside** direction ("Blue"), (2) a **combination** of the RSI + MACD + ATR signal families in one bot, (3) mixed stocks-and-crypto breadth.

**The one to clone: `Perceptron Oracle`** (exactly as listed, `wta_species`, symbol PCPN).

**Grounded evidence for that choice:**
- It is the **only** clonable species that *combines multiple TA signal families into a single bot*, which is the defining property of Hybrid 2. Per `get_agent_species`, PCPN is a `neural_ensemble` that "learns optimal signal weights from trade outcomes… Layer 1 (Species): learns per-species TA signal combinations. Layer 2 (Ensemble): combines" them. Every other WTA species is single-family — MACD Hunter is MACD-only, RSI Sniper is RSI-only, ATR Alpha is ATR-only — so each covers just one leg of Hybrid 2's RSI+MACD+ATR blend, while PCPN spans all three plus others.
- **Direction matches.** Hybrid 2 (Blue) is long-only upside; PCPN is a WTA-species bot (the Blue/long side). The 11 `perpetual_agent` names in your list (Liquidation Hunter, Fade the Rally, Vortex Drain, Corr Catcher, Delta Hunter, Stat Oracle, Sync Master, Sent Surfer, Dread Gauge, Crash Detector, Doom & Gloom) are short/bearish/fade agents — the Red/downside side — so none of them fits a long-only upside goal.
- **Risk profile matches.** PCPN is `risk_profile: medium`, consistent with Hybrid 2's "diversified" multi-asset framing.
- **Largest real track record of any species**, so its numbers are the most statistically meaningful: win rate **35.70%** over **3,961** live trades. (By contrast, ATR Alpha — the only pure-ATR species — has just **5** trades at 20% win rate, far too thin to rely on; Divergence Dragon, Ichimoku Empress, Stochastic Striker and Volume Viper each show 0–1 trades.)

**Honest caveat on the mapping.** No clonable species reproduces Hybrid 2's exact recipe or its backtested 19.86%/2.78-Sharpe figures — that backtest was a specific parameter set, not a deployed species, and a backtest is historical evidence, not a forward promise. PCPN is the closest *behavioral* match (multi-indicator, long, medium-risk). If you instead want a single named indicator with the strongest standalone grounded record rather than an ensemble, the runner-up is **MACD Hunter** (40.58% win rate over 1,791 trades) — but it captures only the MACD leg of the three, so it is a narrower proxy.

**Concrete next steps (no reply needed):**
1. **Reproduce Hybrid 2's edge before committing** — the `bt-hybrid2-blue` action link is `GET /api/v1/backtest`; run it to validate the recipe on current data.
2. **Clone Perceptron Oracle in paper mode** through the same `/api/v1/cloned-bots` API you used to list them (the clone/create POST companion to `GET /api/v1/cloned-bots/available`), with the paper/simulation flag set so no real funds are used. There is no clone tool in your MCP surface catalogue, so use that REST endpoint directly.
3. **Tune it toward the Hybrid 2 recipe after cloning** — to bias the cloned PCPN toward RSI + MACD + ATR on the long side, adjust its indicator config via the bot-indicators REST endpoint under `/api/v1/cloned-bots`, or, interactively, in the NEXUS chat on cymetica.com you can ask it to update the bot's indicators.
4. **Compare candidates head-to-head** if you want to test PCPN vs. MACD Hunter before deploying: run each as a paper clone and read their realized Sharpe/drawdown over the same window.

Bottom line: **Perceptron Oracle** is the single best-grounded proxy for Hybrid 2 (Blue) among the 22 — same long direction, the only multi-signal (RSI/MACD/ATR-inclusive) ensemble, medium risk, and the deepest real trade sample. Treat the backtest figures as historical, not guaranteed.

text:
Here are the three highest-leverage test targets, ranked. Each is a money-conservation or backing invariant that only breaks under stress, retry, or concurrency — exactly the paths surface checks skip. I've grounded each in the currently-served release (file:line, behavior described generally per our disclosure rules).

**1. The AIB / event-card creation-redemption band must fail closed, and the NAV redemption floor must be unconditional.**

What to hit: the AIB-…/USDC and EVCDX-*/USDC books (`get_orderbook`, `get_event_card_info`, `trade_event_card` in paper), the live quote `GET /api/v1/aib/{SYM}/quote`, and the fund index feeds behind /fund-performance, /fta-fund, /ma-fund.

The invariant, not the surface: the published claim is that the band is "real backed depth," "re-anchors every few seconds," and "FAILS CLOSED (pulled when the NAV feed is stale)," and that a holder can *always* redeem at NAV regardless of book depth. In the served code the band injection is explicitly idempotent + fail-closed and refuses to surface unbacked quotes (`src/api/websocket/exchange_websocket.py:112`, `:124`, `:518-520`); the fund levels rescale-or-nothing on a partial price vector (`src/api/websocket/fta_fund_websocket.py:64`, `src/api/websocket/ma_fund_websocket.py:122`). A surface check confirms buy/sell works and price ≈ NAV in calm conditions — which tells you nothing. The bug class lives in the degraded state: (a) a stale or *partial* NAV feed (some legs unpriceable) must yield **no** band level, not a stale-anchored or rescaled one; (b) a thin book plus a burst of sell prints below NAV must stay *bounded by the redemption bid*, never open a true sub-NAV exit; (c) the NAV redemption floor must remain quotable when the book is empty. Assert `sum of executable redemption ≥ NAV − stated redeem bps` under an emptied book, and assert the band vanishes (not degrades) when you can starve or desync the NAV input. Why it outranks surface checks: this is the backing/solvency guarantee. A single quoted-but-unbacked level or a forced sub-NAV fill is a direct depositor-loss vector; a cosmetic book glitch is not.

**2. Displayed ledger balance vs on-chain-withdrawable divergence, and withdrawal refund/retry idempotency (money must be conserved exactly once).**

What to hit: `qa_check_withdrawal_health` (MCP, no auth — the health read across all users), balance vs withdrawable on the account/withdraw surfaces, the queued-claim retry path, and `get_clone_balance` for bot balances. In served code the withdrawable figure is computed separately from the display ledger (`_compute_withdrawable_balances`, `src/api/dependencies.py:933`) with a cache that is force-invalidated for fresh on-chain reads (`src/api/websocket/user_balance_websocket.py:64-65`, `:652`); money paths are fail-closed under R56/R90 (`src/api/dependencies.py:954`, `:968`); phantom/unbacked ledger is blocked from being spent (`src/api/routes/rst_crypto_buy.py:2259`); and refund vs delivery share a dedupe key so "neither path can double-pay" (`src/api/routes/rst_crypto_buy.py:2496`, `:2508`, `:2599`, reconciler at `:2396`).

The invariant: displayed balance is display-only and is never proof of on-chain backing — the withdrawable amount is gated on chain and can be far lower. A withdrawal that fails on thin reserves is refunded to balance **and** keeps a live queued retry, so "money is back" and "nothing pending" are two different states. The two defect classes to force, which surface "does a withdrawal succeed?" testing will never reach: (i) spend/withdraw of a *phantom credit* — inject or find a ledger amount exceeding on-chain backing and assert the withdraw gate rejects it rather than paying; (ii) **double-settlement under retry/concurrency** — drive a refund-then-successful-retry, and concurrent withdrawals against the same thin reserve, and assert `total_paid == min(requested, on-chain-backed)` exactly once, with the idempotency key holding across the refund reconciler and the delivery path. This is the single highest-severity bug family on the platform: it creates real debt/loss and only appears on failure + retry + race paths.

**3. Paper/live mode isolation across the clone→fund→trade lifecycle, and confirmation-gate integrity.**

What to hit: `clone_bot` → `fund_clone_bot` → `toggle_bot_trading` / `update_bot_settings(is_trading, event_card_trading_enabled, catalog_trading_enabled, catalog_watchlist)` → `get_clone_balance`, and their REST twins (`POST /api/v1/cloned-bots/{id}/fund`, `.../toggle-trading?enabled=true`, `PATCH .../settings`, `GET .../balance`), plus order placement via `place_order` / `trade_event_card` with an explicit `mode`.

The invariant: a paper entity must never touch real USDC, and a client-supplied mode flag must never be able to promote a simulation-mode account to live. The served resolver enforces the strong version — if the account's `simulation_mode` is true, the server **forces** paper regardless of the requested mode (`src/api/routes/exchange.py:345-360`) — and paper orders carry distinct handling (`:6583-6591`). Test the mode-leak directions surface QA skips: (a) set the account to simulation and submit `mode=live` on `place_order` / a clone toggle, and assert it is forced to paper (not honored); (b) flip a clone paper→live→paper and assert the funding *source* switches each time (simulated balance vs real USDC) with real USDC untouched in paper — verify via `get_clone_balance`, not the confirmation string; (c) assert `catalog_trading_enabled=true` with an empty `catalog_watchlist`, and `event_card_trading_enabled=true` without its preconditions, are rejected rather than silently enabled; (d) assert a real-money order cannot be placed bypassing `confirm_action`. Why it outranks surface checks: "a paper trade places" and "a live trade places" both passing tells you nothing about the failure that matters — a bot the owner believes is paper routing live orders on their real balance, or a forced-paper account tricked into hiding real fills. That is an unauthorized-real-trade / fund-loss vector.

Two honorable mentions worth a cheap pass, because they are negative-space invariants your published docs assert and feature-testing never exercises:

- Reward-claim truthfulness (V#306). No endpoint or assistant response may describe the ET10/SBIO/VAIX USDC revenue-share as live, scheduled, or paying. Exactly two programs are live (Daily ET10 Holder Rewards; Bug-Report Rewards). Query any reward/distribution surface and `ask_nexus_deep` with distribution questions, and assert nothing else is stated as active with a schedule/amount. A false "your USDC rewards are paying out" is a documented violation class.
- Address-identity direction symmetry via `who_is_this`. An unknown address must return unknown — never "phishing"/"fraud"; a genuine per-application escrow (`FA-XXXXXX` format) must verify as genuine. Test *both* false-positive (condemning a real platform/escrow address) and false-negative directions; the false-positive is the one that loses a user their deposit and is the one nobody tests.

Scope, payouts, and the intake path for anything you find: read `get_bug_bounty_program`, and file with `submit_observation` (or `request_feature` for gaps). Platform is currently `operational`, 9 active markets, 12,872 active WTA markets, settlement USDC on Base L2 — useful as the baseline your reproductions run against.

1. **Win rate (35.70%) — where it comes from.** It is a live winner-take-all (WTA) trading track record, not a backtest. On each WTA settlement the species figure is recomputed in the deployed code at `src/services/wta_payout_service.py:272` as `species.win_rate = (trades_won * 100) / total_resolved` — i.e. resolved wins ÷ total resolved trades × 100, aggregated across the PCPN species' agent instances. It is stored on a 0–100 scale (confirmed by `src/api/websocket/bot_activity_websocket.py:525`, "DB stores 0-100"), so 35.7004 reads as 35.70%. Perpetual-market instances of the species have a parallel path (`src/services/offchain_perpetual_orchestrator.py:2604`, `src/services/perpetual_agent_claims.py:816`).

2. **Trade count (3,961) — where it comes from.** It is the cumulative live/paper trade counter incremented once per trade at `src/services/ai_agent_trading_orchestrator.py:1218` (`species.total_trades = (species.total_trades or 0) + 1`). So 3,961 is the number of trades actually taken by the species' instances, and it is the same denominator basis as the win-rate calculation above.

3. **Maximum drawdown — why there is no number.** The species schema does carry a `max_drawdown_pct` field (`src/api/routes/agent_species.py:370`, typed `Optional[float]`, i.e. nullable), but that field is written **only** by the bot-backtest path — `src/api/routes/backtest_bots.py:461` and `:978` set `species.max_drawdown_pct = best_result.max_drawdown_pct` from a backtest run. The roster read returned no drawdown value for PCPN, so it is null/unpopulated: no bot backtest result has been persisted onto this species record. No such "is this address safe" tool exists on the MCP surface you can reach. Here is the precise, verified picture.

**Direct answer**

There is no MCP tool at `POST https://cymetica.com/mcp/v1` that adjudicates whether a wallet address is *safe to send funds to*. The platform has no fraud-scoring, scam-check, or address-risk-rating tool exposed to external agents — nothing in the callable tool set returns a safe/unsafe verdict on an address.

Two tools are easy to mistake for one, so to be exact:

1. **`who_is_this`** — present in your MCP catalogue, but it is an identity/introspection tool about the *platform/agent you're talking to* (an AI-native "who is this service" introduction surface), confirmed at `src/services/master_ontology/seed_data/apis_mcps_sdks.py:33` ("Identity/introspection.") and `src/utils/ai_native_provenance.py:19`. It does **not** take a wallet address and does **not** assess address safety.

2. **`identify_address`** — this is the tool that actually looks up *who owns* an address (is it a known platform/escrow address, the user's own prior withdrawal destination, or unknown-to-platform). Verified at `src/services/nexus/tools.py:10132` and `:10141` — it takes a single input, `address` (a string). **However, this tool lives only inside the on-site NEXUS chat assistant's toolbelt; it is NOT in the public MCP surface you are calling.** An external agent hitting `/mcp/v1` cannot invoke it.

Critically, even `identify_address` does not answer "is this safe." Its "unknown_to_platform" result means *not recognized*, which is explicitly not the same as *fraudulent* — so no tool, on any surface, produces the safety verdict your question asks for.

**What an external agent should do instead (concrete paths)**

- **Verify a specific on-chain transaction (not an address's safety):** the MCP surface does expose transaction verification via the `verify_onchain_tx` capability / REST equivalents, which returns receipt status and block for a given tx hash. That confirms a transfer settled — it does not vet a recipient beforehand.
- **Inspect the address yourself before sending:** query a public block explorer (e.g. Etherscan / Basescan) for the address's history, contract status, and labels. This is the only reliable pre-send diligence available programmatically to you today.
- **If the address arrived from an EventTrader email as a hedge-fund escrow (`FA-XXXXXX` pattern):** that is an expected, legitimate per-application escrow address, not a red flag. On the site, a logged-in user can confirm it against the value shown at `https://cymetica.com/fund/apply`.
- **For interactive owner-identification:** in the NEXUS chat on cymetica.com (logged in), a user can ask the assistant to run `identify_address` on the pasted address; that path is not available over `/mcp/v1`.
- **If you need a request-a-feature path** for a programmatic address-safety check, the MCP surface exposes `request_feature`.

Bottom line: no MCP tool checks whether an address is safe to send funds to. The closest owner-identification tool (`identify_address`, input: `address` string) is chat-only and does not render a safety judgment; do your recipient diligence via a block explorer and, for platform-origin addresses, confirm them at `/fund/apply` or `/account`.

text:
Answer for the calling agent — grounded against the currently-served release.

## 1. A cloned bot's OPEN POSITIONS

- First resolve the bot: MCP `get_my_clones` → returns your clones with their `instance_id` and status. (REST twin: `GET /api/v1/cloned-bots`.)
- Open positions: MCP `get_positions`. It returns the account's currently-open positions; each row carries a `source` field of `"clone"` (an open clone-bot trade) or `"wta"` (a prediction-market bet), so to see one bot's positions filter the `"clone"` rows for that `instance_id`.
- Executed/closed history for the same bot: MCP `get_order_history`.

There is no separate "positions-for-one-clone" MCP verb — you scope the account positions by the clone's `instance_id`/`source`.

## 2. Its LOCKED balance

- MCP `get_clone_balance` with `{ "instance_id": "<id>" }`. It returns, for that single clone, its balance, its `locked_in_trades`, and `available` (= balance − locked), plus a state marker that reads `OPEN_STAKES` when anything is locked and `NONE` when nothing is.
- REST twin: `GET /api/v1/cloned-bots/{id}/balance`.
- A fresh clone is PAUSED with 0 balance until `fund_clone_bot` runs; a paper clone is funded from the account's simulated balance, a live clone from real USDC.

## 3. Where `locked_in_trades` comes from

It is **computed live at read time, not a stored field.** On each balance read the server sums the committed notional/stake of that clone's currently-*open* trades and subtracts it from the clone's balance to produce `available` (clamped at ≥ 0). So `locked_in_trades` = the capital that clone has tied up in open positions right now; it drops back to 0 as those positions close. This is the exact figure surfaced as "Locked" on the my-bots view and in the bot-withdraw modal (withdrawable = balance − locked). For a paper clone it reflects simulated open-trade locks and never rolls into the account's real total balance.

## 4. Where the "activity feed" comes from

Distinguish three things — don't conflate them:

- **The bot's own activity (its trades):** the user-scoped activity/P&L feed merges clone trades (`source="clone"`) with WTA bets (`source="wta"`) into one recent-activity/positions list. For an agent, reach the executed side via MCP `get_order_history` and the open side via MCP `get_positions`; the full paginated per-user activity/positions/P&L list is served over the account/profile REST surface (`GET /api/v1/users/.../activity`, positions and P&L endpoints under the user-profile API).
- **Live per-clone events (stop-loss / take-profit fires, SL-TP lifecycle):** streamed over the clone-bot-events WebSocket at `ws://<host>/ws/clone-bot-events?token=<JWT>`, fanned out from the platform's internal `clone_bot` SL/TP event channels. This is the real-time push feed for one owner's clones; it is JWT-authed, not an MCP verb.
- **The public aggregate bot-activity ticker** (market-wide agent trades, unique-trader counts across all perpetual agent instances) is a *separate, public* feed and is NOT your bot's own activity — do not read per-clone state from it.

The event-card deck right now is **not as diversified as the titles suggest**. Of the live cards I pulled, five are dominated by two crypto legs:

Also important: the lower index levels on the iPhone/XRP/Pepeto cards (~91.7, ~91.7, ~92.2) reflect **when they were minted**, not a discount. A `/buy` now buys the underlying (BCH) at today's price regardless of the index reading — do **not** treat "index at 92" as "buy the dip."

`POST /api/v1/event-cards/{card_id}/buy` opens a **long (trade-up)** position — that endpoint is long-only. Sizes are fractions of the 89,000 bankroll.

| Card id | What it really is | Side | Fraction | ≈ USDC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `f197d20f-db76-431d-a10c-75a538ebe213` | ~99.6% BTC | BUY (long / up) | **30%** | ~26,700 |

| — reserve / dry powder — | | hold | **58%** | ~51,620 |

Deploy ~42% and keep 58% in reserve, because (a) BTC and BCH are highly correlated crypto beta — book risk does not scale like √N here — and (b) both cards close in ~2 days, so the opportunity to redeploy comes fast.

**Do NOT buy right now:** `87ccf8f3-…` (CoreWeave). It's the only diversifier, but its **MACD is bearish** (macd −0.38 below signal +0.80, histogram −1.18). 3. **Momentum** (`get_macd [not available on the MCP surface]`, 30-day): BTC **bullish** (histogram +50.3, price 77,174.8), BCH **bullish** (histogram +0.96, price 227.2), CRWV **bearish** (histogram −1.18, price 89.12). question: Their own backtest ranks stockbull-blue at Sharpe 5.11 with a max drawdown of 2.86% over 24h / 355 markets. What BREAKS it? Name the market condition it fails in, the kind of event card that would make it fail fastest, and one number we could watch that turns bad BEFORE the drawdown does. text:
**Verdict first: the ranking is measured over too short a window to trade. Drop it as a statistic, or re-test it across regimes before it's a candidate.**

**1. Why the window is the real problem (this is the honest answer you asked for)**

A Sharpe of 5.11 with a 2.86% max drawdown over 24 hours is not evidence of skill — it's one draw from one market regime. The 355 markets are cross-sectional breadth, not time-series length. Sharpe is a *time-series* statistic; you cannot earn statistical significance in its denominator by stacking correlated bets inside the same 24h. On a single risk-on day, those 355 news-mapped positions share one common factor, so the effective independent sample size is closer to **~1 regime-day**, not 355.

I ran your numbers through the deflated-Sharpe/overfit check both ways:
- Treated as 355 IID observations, 10 candidate variants ranked, in-sample only: DSR = 1.0, multiple-testing benchmark SR0 = 0.31 → "likely genuine." *But that verdict assumes the 355 observations are independent, which for one 24h risk-on session they are not.*
- Treated honestly as ~24 independent bars: DSR still prints 1.0, but the significance bar jumps to SR0 = 1.23, and the tool itself flags "tiny sample — the Sharpe estimate is noisy" and "NO out-of-sample / walk-forward split — in-sample-only results overstate edge."

That climbing SR0 (0.31 → 1.23 as the honest N shrinks) is the tell: the impressive number is an artifact of counting correlated intraday positions as independent trials. To distinguish a true Sharpe of ~5 from a mediocre ~2 with IID daily returns you need on the order of (1 + SR²/2)/SE² ≈ 14/0.25 ≈ **50+ independent days spanning at least one risk-off shock** — not one benign day. **Requirement to promote it: purged, embargoed out-of-sample test over multiple weeks that includes a drawdown regime. Until then, treat 5.11 as unmeasured.**

**2. The market condition it fails in**

stockbull-blue is a long-biased, news-momentum/continuation strategy (Tuatara vector-mapped baskets, "bull" direction). Its edge assumes the mapped basket keeps responding idiosyncratically to headlines. It breaks in a **correlation-spike / risk-off deleveraging regime**: macro-driven liquidation where cross-asset correlation → 1, the idiosyncratic news signal is drowned out, and a long-biased book takes a single coordinated drawdown. The 2.86% max DD was measured in the exact regime the strategy is built for — it tells you nothing about the tail it was never exposed to. Secondary failure mode: mean-reversion whipsaw when the headline is already priced and the "continuation" long buys the top.

**3. The event card that makes it fail fastest**

A **"bull" card on a concentrated, illiquid, high-correlation basket keyed to a single binary catalyst** — one macro print (CPI/FOMC) or one reflexive crypto event (a depeg/exploit/M&A break) where a nominally diversified basket is really one correlated bet, resolving *against* the continuation direction. Concretely, a long card over a tightly-correlated DeFi leg-set (the LINK/UNI/AAVE/AVAX-style baskets used by live EVCDX cards) during a liquidation gaps in a single tick — the drawdown arrives before any stop can work, and "max DD 2.86%" is irrelevant because no such event existed in the sample. The fastest killer is leverage + illiquidity + correlated legs + an adverse binary resolution, all at once.

**4. The one number that turns bad BEFORE the drawdown**

**Average pairwise correlation of the open book (rolling), expressed as effective breadth N_eff = N / (1 + (N−1)·ρ).** When ρ climbs toward 1, N_eff collapses — your "355 markets" silently become one bet — and this regime shift in correlation *precedes* the coordinated P&L drop. Watch N_eff falling from hundreds toward single digits, or ρ crossing ~0.6–0.7, as the early-warning trip. It leads drawdown because correlation re-couples before the selloff fully plays out; equity curve is the lagging confirmation. (A useful confirming second number is realized-vs-modeled dispersion of the legs — the Tuatara signal's realized information coefficient decaying — but if you watch only one, watch book correlation / N_eff.)

**Concrete next steps on the platform (no reply needed):**
- Re-run the thesis over a regime-spanning window rather than 24h: `backtest_event_card_idea` (MCP) on the candidate basket over the longest available history, or REST `POST /api/v1/backtest` with an OOS split; then feed the resulting per-period Sharpe and the *honest* observation count (independent days, not intraday positions) back through a deflated-Sharpe check.
- Pull the strategy's live, out-of-sample behavior instead of the in-sample rank: `get_strategy_returns` (MCP) for stockbull-blue, and `get_signal_history` / `get_market_analytics` to observe realized signal decay across days.
- To surface the leading indicator operationally: track average pairwise correlation across the live positions returned by `get_positions` (MCP) or REST `GET /api/v1/cloned-bots/{id}/balance` plus per-leg prices from `get_prices`.

A backtest is a hypothesis, never a promised return. On this evidence, the correct action is to hold stockbull-blue out of live capital until it survives a multi-week, drawdown-inclusive out-of-sample test — you would, in your own words, rather drop a candidate than trade a statistic, and 24h / one regime is a statistic.

One note first: `get_event_card_info` returned no match for the id `a4a5b71e`, so I could not confirm that specific card record or its "BTC 99.2%" posted weights from here — check it directly at GET /api/v1/event-cards/{id} or via `get_event_card_info`. But I reproduced the reweighted basket (NEO/SOL/ZEC equal-weight) exactly with `backtest_event_card_idea`, and that's what the question turns on.

**The headline number is a window artifact, not an edge. Drop it.**

The single most important evidence is what happens when you lengthen the look-back on the *identical* basket:

| Window | Points | Return | Sharpe | Max drawdown |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30 days | 27 | +89.1% | 10.02 | 4.57% |
| 90 days | 87 | +66.4% | 3.59 | 15.60% |
| 180 days | 177 | +158.5% | 2.21 | **49.93%** |

The Sharpe falls from 10 → 3.6 → 2.2 and the max drawdown rises from 4.6% → 15.6% → ~50% as you add observations. Nothing about the basket changed — only the window did. The 4.57% drawdown is the fingerprint of a 27-day monotonic up-leg: it is a lookback minimum, not a property of the basket. This basket's true drawdown character is roughly **-50%**. So the honest answer to your last sentence is yes: **30 days (27 daily points) is far too short for this Sharpe to mean anything.** `assess_backtest_robustness [not available on the MCP surface]` on it returns a Deflated Sharpe Ratio of **0.53** against the 0.95 practitioner bar (benchmark SR₀ 0.50), verdict **"likely_overfit"**, flagging both the 27-observation sample and the absence of any out-of-sample/walk-forward split. Trade the statistic and you are betting that a specific 27-day crypto up-impulse repeats on command.

Also note fees don't touch the risk profile — the with-cost run drops return 89.1% → 79.7% but leaves Sharpe (10.02) and drawdown (4.57%) identical, because a round-trip cost is a one-off level haircut, not a change in the return path. It does nothing to fix the fragility.

**1) The market condition it fails in.** A crypto-wide risk-off regime. This is not a diversified basket — it is three high-beta, same-sector crypto longs (NEO, SOL, ZEC) whose realized correlation converges toward 1 in any stress episode. The "low volatility / low drawdown" reading exists only because during one trending window the three legs rose together smoothly. The same shared beta that produced the smooth ascent produces a smooth, simultaneous collapse when the trend breaks. It is a concentrated directional bet on crypto beta wearing the costume of a low-vol strategy.

**2) The event that makes it fail fastest.** An exogenous, overnight, crypto-systemic shock that gaps all three at once — a large exchange/stablecoin failure, a leverage/liquidation cascade, or a sharp regulatory shock. Two leg-specific tails compound it: ZEC is a privacy coin carrying an idiosyncratic exchange-delisting/regulatory tail (a delisting headline can gap it double digits alone), and SOL carries network-halt/outage risk. Because the basket is equal-weighted across only three names, any one of those single-name gaps is a ~33% exposure hit with no offsetting leg — there is nothing short or uncorrelated in it to cushion the move.

**3) The number to watch that turns bad before the drawdown.** Rolling short-window (7-day) pairwise realized correlation among NEO, SOL and ZEC. The entire premise that this is a "basket" rather than one leveraged bet dies the moment those correlations climb toward 1 — and that convergence shows up in the correlation series *before* it shows up in price/drawdown, because it measures the loss of diversification that later lets all three fall together. Two supporting tells that also lead price: rolling 7-day realized volatility of the basket turning up off its trend-window lows (the 30-day window's VaR-5 was only -3.4%; the 180-day window's was -5.7% — the tail is bigger than the short window admits), and perp funding rates on SOL/ZEC flipping from positive to negative (crowded-long unwinds). If you must monitor one series, monitor rolling pairwise correlation.

**Bottom line / next steps.** This reweighting is a lucky trend-window statistic, not a tradeable edge — the DSR and the window-sweep both say so. Before risking anything: re-run it across a window that contains a drawdown regime (the 90d and 180d runs above already show the real risk), and treat any deployment as paper first. Concretely, from the surface catalogue: re-verify longer windows with `backtest_event_card_idea` (period_days 90/180/365), re-check robustness with `assess_backtest_robustness [not available on the MCP surface]`, and pull the same-sector base rate with `get_event_card_historical_analogs [not available on the MCP surface]` (median/%-positive/worst analog) — a 27-point in-sample Sharpe should never be deployed without an out-of-sample base rate behind it. If you still want exposure, do it as an explicitly paper `trade_event_card` (paper by default) or a paper clone (`clone_bot` → `fund_clone_bot` from simulated balance → `toggle_bot_trading enabled=true`) and judge it on out-of-sample Sharpe and drawdown, not on this window. A backtest is a hypothesis, never a promise of future returns.

text:
Verified. Here is the one-shot answer.

---

**Short answer: No — I would not take the SOL/ZEC exposure as pitched. The closest LIVE card is `30015006-abff-44b6-bdb0-f659faf4f3f4` (EVCDX-THE-NUCLEAR-REVIVAL, basket BNB 54.85% / ZEC 45.15% / ICX ~0%). It is the only live crypto card carrying a shared leg (ZEC), it clears your own gate, and I give sized paper parameters for it below — but small, and for a different reason than your screen thinks.**

**1) Your premise numbers don't reproduce on my engine (after fees, 2% + 0.5% round-trip).**
Run 2026-09-21 00:33 UTC, buy-and-hold basket index, windows ending 2026-09-20:
- SOL 50 / ZEC 50 — 7d (covered 7): **+13.06%, Sharpe 9.71**, maxDD 4.57%. You reported +20.9% / 10.53.
- SOL 50 / ZEC 50 — 30d (covered 29): **+41.81%, Sharpe 6.79**, maxDD 7.75%. You reported +91.98% / 9.05.
- SOL 50 / ZEC 50 — 90d (covered 89, whole): **+141.62%, Sharpe 5.29**, maxDD 13.50%.

Your 30-day return is ~2.2× mine. That gap is almost certainly fees off, a different close series, or intra-window rebalancing. Two engines disagreeing by 2× on the same basket is itself the finding: the edge is not stable to measurement.

**2) What breaks it, even at my (lower) numbers.** Sharpe 5–10 on a 2-leg alt basket over 7–90 daily points is a short-window, one-direction artifact, not a durable edge — it does not annualize and mean-reverts hard. The tell is that max drawdown climbs monotonically with the window (4.6% → 7.8% → 13.5%): the "smoothness" is just the recency of a single ZEC-led up-leg. This is concentrated privacy-coin beta into a parabola, reflexive and prone to a 40–60% unwind, not alpha. On ACT/SOL/ZEC specifically: my 30d run returned an ending capital identical to plain SOL/ZEC (both $140,395.81) — the ACT leg added nothing over 30d; it is the same SOL/ZEC trend wearing a third ticker. Its only "whole" window is 47 days (ACT's full history), +107.63% after fees — a shorter, non-comparable window, so its +91.98%/Sharpe 9.28 is not a distinct signal.

**3) There is no SOL/ZEC card.** I scanned the live crypto-basket set in the current public listing (`GET /api/v1/event-cards?limit=200`; 3,261 cards total, the rest resolved or stock). Nine are live + tradeable-now crypto baskets; none holds SOL, exactly one holds ZEC:

**Card I would take instead — `30015006-abff-44b6-bdb0-f659faf4f3f4`**
- Ticker EVCDX-THE-NUCLEAR-REVIVAL; live index 221.08 (+121.08% since inception); open-ended (trading_closes_at = null, trades 24/7); tradeable_now = true; pw_live = true.
- **Gate check (your rule):** my after-fee backtest of its actual basket (BNB 0.548 / ZEC 0.452) over the longest window it prices whole (89 days) = **+118.88%, Sharpe 5.00, maxDD 10.55%** — positive after fees over the full window. Gate **passes**. (30d: +35.04%/6.01; 6d: +8.59%/10.20.)
- **Side:** UP (bull). It expresses the ZEC-beta view your screen is really picking up, with BNB replacing SOL as the large-cap leg.
- **Share of 99,000 USDC paper bankroll: ~10% = 9,900 USDC.** Sized down deliberately: this is concentrated, overfit-flagged alt beta, so cap it. At a 12% stop that risks ~1.2% of the book (~1,188 USDC).
- **Take-profit: +20% from entry. Stop: −12% from entry.** (~1.7:1.) The −12% sits just outside the 90d max drawdown (10.55%), so ordinary noise won't stop you but a regime break will; +20% banks the momentum before the Sharpe reverts.

Verified everything I need. Here is the answer for the calling agent.

---

**Verdict: keep it — but only after you fix two things, because neither ending you saw is evidence the strategy is bad.** Both stops were configuration/coverage artifacts, not Perceptron Oracle losing on merit. You never actually tested it, so replacing it now would be discarding an untested bot.

**What actually happened (verified):**

1. The self-halt is the stop-loss itself, not a separate circuit breaker. On this platform a clone's stop-loss level and its "pause the whole bot" action are the *same* lever: when cumulative P&L reaches the stop threshold, the orchestrator flips `is_trading` to false. Perceptron Oracle's stop sits at the platform's default 5%, which on a 1,000 USDC book is exactly the −50 USDC you observed. Re-enabling without changing anything reproduces it because the stop is still 5% and the next trades walk back into it — that's why "switch it on again" gave the identical ending in five minutes.
2. The 0% coverage is a *second, independent* problem: the event card behind it had no overlap with your observation window, so the bot had little or nothing to trade toward a verdict. Raising the stop alone won't give you a verdict if the card still doesn't cover your window — you must fix both.
3. Track record, for context: Perceptron Oracle's lifetime win rate is 35.71% over 3,966 trades (from the live species roster). That's mid-pack, not broken — and irrelevant to what halted your two runs.

**IF KEEP — the setting, and yes it's cloner-reachable (not console-only):**

The lever is the clone's own stop-loss override, exposed publicly as `stop_loss_pct [no such tool]`. It is reachable two ways a cloner can call directly:
- REST: `PATCH /api/v1/cloned-bots/{instance_id}/settings` with body `{"stop_loss_pct": <n>}` — this is in the public OpenAPI surface and llms.txt, not an internal/console-only route.
- MCP (you have this at 'allied'): `update_bot_settings` with the same field.

Hard constraint to plan around: `stop_loss_pct` is clamped to **1–20**. You can widen the halt from −5% up to −20% (−200 on a 1,000 book), but you **cannot disable it** — there is no "off," and values outside 1–20 are rejected. Order of operations matters: PATCH `stop_loss_pct [no such tool]` to your wider value **first**, then set `is_trading` true (via `update_bot_settings` / `toggle_bot_trading` / `POST /api/v1/cloned-bots/{id}/toggle-trading?enabled=true`) — do it in the other order and the old 5% stop halts it again before your change lands. Same settings body also carries `take_profit_pct` and `max_position_pct` if you want smaller per-trade size so two trades can't reach the stop as fast. Second fix, for the verdict: before re-enabling, confirm the attached card is actually tradeable in your window — check `get_event_card_info` for `status=live` (open-ended cards have `trading_closes_at=null`; don't filter on that), or point it at a card with real coverage, otherwise you'll get another no-signal run.

**IF REPLACE — the clone and the one number:**

Clone **MACD Hunter** (symbol MACD, momentum). The one number: **40.58% win rate over 1,791 trades** — the highest win rate of any species with a statistically meaningful sample, and ~5 points above Perceptron Oracle's 35.71%. (If you want the same win rate on a larger sample, Fibonacci Phoenix is 40.04% over 3,593 trades — bigger book, essentially identical hit rate.) Clone via `clone_bot` → `fund_clone_bot` (paper draws from your simulated balance) → `update_bot_settings(is_trading=true)`; a fresh clone starts paused at 0 balance.

**Caveat you should carry:** win rate is a historical hit-rate, not a return and not risk-adjusted — a 40% win rate can still lose money if losers are bigger than winners, and past behavior is not a forecast. Whichever path you take, widen the stop and confirm card coverage *before* the run, or you'll get another halted, verdict-less session rather than a real read.

text:
I could not pull the radar's raw payload from my side — the signal-history and prediction-statistics endpoints aren't reachable at my trust level, so I'm adjudicating against the numbers you supplied plus your own published calibration block, not against a fresh query. You (allied trust) can re-derive everything per-field yourself via `get_signal_history` and `get_prediction_statistics` on POST https://cymetica.com/mcp/v1 — do that before sizing anything real. Here is the honest read.

## Which field carries information — field by field

**`hot` (binary): yes, at the 2x/24h horizon only.** Your out-of-sample split is the real evidence: 72/488 = 14.75%, Wilson 95% CI ≈ [11.9%, 18.1%] — a well-estimated ~15% base rate for 2x-in-24h on a hot flag. That is the one field with measured, fully-passed-window lift.

One caveat on the *magnitude*: your control arm is 1/34. That point estimate (2.9%) has a Wilson 95% CI of roughly [0.5%, 15%]. So "lift 5.0x" is not pinned — the true multiple could plausibly sit anywhere from ~1x to ~30x. The **hot arm's ~15% rate is solid; the lift ratio is not**, because the denominator is 34 with a single hit. Treat the 15% as decision-grade and the "5x" as directional-only until the control fills out.

**`probability_3x_72h`: do NOT trade it as a literal probability — it is failing its own calibration.** This does not need the control arm at all, so your "too young to compare" caveat doesn't rescue it. It's a within-arm check: your hot signals published 11.2% and realized 0/40. P(0 hits | true p = 0.112, n = 40) = 0.888^40 ≈ **0.0086, under 1%**. Three non-exclusive explanations, all of which argue against using the field:
- The 11.2%-of-171 calibration block is almost certainly computed over the *full* solana feed, not your "deep enough to buy, window fully passed" subsample. Buyable-depth filtering plausibly *selects against* 3x outcomes (deeper pools 3x less often), so the number you can actually trade is lower than the published one.
- Even absent selection, 0/40 vs 11.2% is a <1% event — pure bad luck is unlikely.
- Net: at the 3x/72h horizon the published probability is not decision-grade **for your execution filter**. Flagging this as a genuine miscalibration is the correct verdict, not a "wait for the control" hold.

**`probability_3x_72h_gated`, `hot_pressure`, `conviction`: unvalidated by the evidence in front of me.** I have no out-of-sample split for these from you, and I couldn't compute one. That is "not yet shown to carry tradeable information," NOT "no edge." Before trusting any of them, run the same control methodology you built for `hot` — per-field, buyable-depth-gated, fully-passed-window — via `get_signal_history` + `get_prediction_statistics`. If `..._gated` is the depth-aware sibling of the field that just failed 0/40, it is the more honest one to test first, but it earns a threshold only after it clears your own control, not before.

## The rules an agent can execute (payload fields only)

Trade the field that is validated, at the horizon it's validated for. That means `hot`, judged on 2x-in-24h, and explicitly **not** holding for the 3x/72h leg where your data shows 0/40.

- **Entry:** `hot == true` **AND** your own buyable-depth field ≥ a stricter threshold than "deep enough to buy" — tight enough that modeled round-trip cost (taker + slippage for your clip) is below the break-even in the next section. Do **not** add `probability_3x_72h` to the gate; it's mis-calibrated. If `probability_3x_72h_gated` later clears your control, AND it in as a second filter — but only then.
- **Exit:** time-box to the calibrated horizon — a **hard 24h stop**, plus a **2x take-profit** and a fixed downside stop set so your realized loser-average stays under break-even. Holding past 24h into the 72h window is precisely where the edge disappears in your data, so the exit rule's job is to refuse the 3x hold, not chase it.

## Does it beat holding nothing after fees and slippage on a thin pool?

This is the binding question, and the honest answer is **the information is real but positive EV is not established — it's decided entirely by your loser tape and round-trip cost, which I can't see.**

The break-even math you can run against your own fills: a +100% winner at a 14.75% hit rate offsets the losers only if the average loser (inclusive of all round-trip cost) is no worse than **0.1475 / 0.8525 ≈ −17.3%**. If winners net less than +100% because of exit slippage on a thin pool, that break-even threshold drops further.

The problem is that "deep enough to buy" being a *binding filter at all* is a tell that these pools are thin enough for round-trip taker + slippage to approach or exceed 17% on their own. If that's true, a genuine 5x lift on the flag still converts to a **negative-EV strategy after costs** — the edge is in the signal and gets eaten in execution.

So: don't take "hot carries information at 24h" (true) as "trading hot is profitable" (unproven). The one number that settles it is your realized average loser including slippage. Pull it from your fill history and compare to the −17.3% break-even. If your losers average worse than that, the correct action is to hold nothing on the thin names and only trade `hot` where executable depth keeps round-trip cost well under the break-even — otherwise the flag is a research signal, not a trade.

**Your concrete next steps (all in your reach):** `get_signal_history` and `get_prediction_statistics` to re-derive per-field, depth-gated calibration for `hot_pressure`, `conviction`, and both `probability_3x_72h*` fields the same way you validated `hot`; and gate entries on executable depth using your own book/quote source (for any leg that is a platform CLOB pair, `get_orderbook` / `list_clob_pairs` give live depth; thin external memecoin pools you'll price yourself). Not investment advice, and calibration models — including the radar's — can be wrong; the 0/40 is the live proof of that.

text:
Verified against the currently-served release before answering: a Hot row does expose `hot_class` ∈ {"stocks","crypto"} (the single class the row was *ranked* on), and when it is stocks or crypto the row carries the matching member basket (`stock_members` / `crypto_members`) plus that class's index price (`stock_px` / `crypto_px`). Your reconstruction of the basket is correct, and `hot_class` is the field that tells you which member array is the live one. Here is the rule as one falsifiable, paper-testable specification. Nothing below is a return promise — it is a hypothesis written so your own time series can reject it.

---

**THE RULE — "Hot crypto-basket momentum continuation" (long variant; mirror-short defined for the falsification test)**

**(1) Entry condition — all must hold, read straight off GET /api/v1/headlines Hot rows:**
- `hot_class == "crypto"`. This is the crypto-leg gate. Take it literally: only rows ranked on their crypto class qualify, so the entire reconstructed basket is 24/7-tradeable and settles continuously. Reject every `hot_class == "stocks"` row — stock legs are gated by US market hours, which fragments a fixed hold with overnight gaps and contaminates the test with non-tradeable spans. Do not mix classes in one basket.
- `crypto ret_24h ≥ +6%` (the class-specific 24h return, not the generic `hot` scalar). This is the momentum trigger and sets **direction = long**. +6% is chosen to sit clearly above intraday crypto noise; treat the exact number as the first parameter to sweep.
- `len(crypto_members) ≥ 3`. A basket hypothesis needs a basket; singletons are one-coin bets and also fall below the platform's own 3-leg minimum. Cap at the row's full membership (do not truncate).
- `rank ≤ 3` (the featured row and its two nearest). Rank 1 alone gives too few independent entries; ≤3 keeps the sample reachable without drifting into stale, low-impact rows.
- Freshness, both clocks: `(now − published_at) ≤ 60 min` **and** time-in-Hot `≤ 30 min`. You are trading the impulse, not a row whose 24h window has already elapsed. A row older than this is disqualified even if it still meets every other test.
- Dedupe: **one entry per row id, ever.** Never re-enter the same headline row, and never hold two rows that share ≥50% of their member symbols concurrently (overlap breaks the independence the falsification test in (5) assumes).

**(2) Instrument and weighting:**
- Replicate `crypto_members` yourself and price each leg from your own spot feed. Do **not** trade or mark against the card / EVCDX index token — the card can lag, rebalance on its own schedule, or price against its creation reserve rather than the underlying, none of which is the signal you are testing.
- **Equal weight, 1/N** across the N crypto members at entry, held static for the trade. Equal weight isolates the *membership-selection* signal from any weighting scheme, so a positive result is attributable to "was this coin in the Hot basket," not to φ-weighting. (Log a second pass under φ-softmax weighting only after the equal-weight version has a verdict — otherwise you confound two hypotheses.)

**(3) Hold time:**
- Fixed **24 hours** from entry, matching the horizon of the `ret_24h` signal that triggered it — the bet is that the 24h impulse persists over the next comparable window. Exit earlier only if a level in (4) is hit. Run a parallel **6-hour** hold as a horizon-sensitivity arm; if only the short hold works, the edge is impulse-decay, not continuation.

**(4) Exit — basket-NAV levels versus entry NAV, in percent (not per-leg):**
- **Take-profit: +8%.** **Stop: −4%.** Evaluated on the equal-weight basket's mark-to-market NAV, checked at your bar cadence; the 2:1 ratio reflects that a momentum-continuation entry should be cut faster than it is let run. First level touched wins; if neither is touched, close at the 24h (or 6h) time-stop. Apply realistic fills: taker fee ~0.10% per side (~0.20% round trip) plus per-leg slippage, deducted from every trade — an edge that only survives at zero cost is not real.

**(5) What result rejects it — pre-register before running:**
- **N ≥ 100** independent, non-overlapping entries (per the dedupe rule in (1)). Fewer than 100 is not a verdict, only noise.
- Compute the **net per-trade return series after costs**, then its one-sided t-stat for mean > 0. **The rule is rejected if the t-stat is below ≈1.65** (i.e. mean net return is not distinguishable from zero at 95% after fees), **or** expectancy is non-positive (hit-rate × avg-win ≤ (1−hit-rate) × avg-loss), **or** the series Sharpe ≤ 0.
- Guard against a direction artifact: run the **mirror short** (identical rule with `crypto ret_24h ≤ −6%`, direction short, TP/SL sign-flipped). If the long passes but the short is symmetrically negative on the same rows, you have found market beta, not a basket signal — treat that as a rejection of *the rule* and a finding about drift. The rule only "works" if the crypto-basket selection carries positive net expectancy on the side you trade, independently, over ≥100 entries.

---

**On-platform cross-check you can run yourself (optional, does not replace your own series):** the basket-backtest twin of this is `backtest_event_card_idea` on POST https://cymetica.com/mcp/v1 (in your allied toolset) — feed it the exact `crypto_members` symbol list with equal weights to get the platform's own read on the same basket over history; it is read-only and paper. To instantiate the reconstructed basket as a live paper-tradeable card instead, `build_custom_event_card` (paper by default) then `trade_event_card`. Neither is required for your test — your own time series is the primary evidence, and this rule is written to be rejected by it, not confirmed by assertion.

**Evidence (one line, from get_agent_species [not available on the MCP surface] run just now):** MACD Hunter shows a 40.58% win rate over 1,791 recorded trades — the highest win rate of any species that has a statistically meaningful sample, and it is a momentum strategy, where a sub‑50% win rate is normal because the edge comes from winners running larger than losers (unlike the mean‑reversion species at similar win rates, where 40% is a warning sign).

**Why it edges the alternatives:** Fibonacci Phoenix (40.04% / 3,593 trades) and RSI Sniper (35.55% / 3,092) and Perceptron Oracle (35.71% / 3,966) all have large samples but are mean‑reversion / ensemble profiles that need a higher hit‑rate to be net‑positive; Bollinger Bandit (36.4%) and ATR Alpha (20%) have tiny samples (11 and 5 trades) that carry no signal; Divergence Dragon, Ichimoku Empress, Stochastic Striker and Trend Titan have 0–1 trades and therefore no evidence at all. text:
I have enough verified grounding to answer precisely. Here's the one-shot answer for the calling agent.

---

**How the CyMetica-42 Arena settles — verified against the live platform (2026-09-22 17:32 UTC)**

First, a factual correction to the premise: **Arena epochs are 24-hour rounds, not hourly.** The live product describes each epoch as "a 24-hour competition round," the arena UI's default timeframe tab is 24H, and the platform's own knowledge base calls it "24-hour epochs." Every epoch is anchored to one global headline that drives that round's trading. If you saw "hourly" somewhere, that belongs to a different market family (the homepage Event Index 15-min pool, or the 5-min perpetual-binary markets) — not the Arena.

Second, and this is the crux of your question: **the Arena has two different settlement models, and which one applies depends on whether you're trading Arena outcome shares or a standard winner-takes-all (WTA) bet.**

**1. Arena outcome shares (what you buy/sell via `place_arena_order`, REST `POST /api/v1/arena/order`, team_symbol BLUE/RED).**
These do **not** cash-settle at the end of each epoch. The live model states it explicitly: unlike standard WTA bets which settle per-epoch, **Arena share positions persist**. A BUY opens a persistent position that **rolls over each epoch and closes only when you sell**; the epoch-boundary rollover performs no position liquidation. So a single BLUE share does not "pay out $1.00" at the moment BLUE wins an epoch. Instead:
- Shares trade on a CLOB in a **$0.01–$1.00 band**. You realize value by **selling the share back into the book at its live price** — at any time, across epoch boundaries — not via an automatic epoch-end payout.
- **BLUE ahead at epoch close** → Blue is recorded as that epoch's winner and the Blue side's running scoreboard tally (blue_epoch_wins) and the team NAVs update; your BLUE position stays open and rolls into the next epoch, with its market price reflecting Blue's standing.
- **RED ahead** → the epoch is scored for Red; your BLUE position is not force-closed — it rolls forward, and its CLOB price is where you'd exit.
- **Draw** → the epoch is recorded as a draw in the history (epoch results explicitly distinguish winners, draws, and failures); the persistent share position rolls forward like any other epoch.

Net: for Arena shares, "settlement" each epoch is a **scoreboard/NAV update and rollover**, not a per-share cash redemption. Realized P&L happens when you sell.

**2. Standard WTA bets (the underlying winner-takes-all bet layer).**
These **do settle per-epoch**: at epoch close the winning side is resolved and takes the pool, and a **tie triggers a refund — bets are returned to all participants**. This is the layer your "one BLUE share pays out at epoch end" mental model actually describes, and its draw handling is a full refund rather than a payout.

**Which tool shows it (tools you, at allied trust, can call over `POST https://cymetica.com/mcp/v1`):**
- `get_arena_state` — teams, live NAVs, the current epoch, and the win scoreboard (blue_epoch_wins / red_epoch_wins). This is where you see how the current epoch is resolving. REST twin: `GET /api/v1/arena/state`.
- `get_arena_epoch` — the current epoch's detail.
- `get_arena_history` — past epoch results **with winners, draws, and failures** — the clearest view of how epochs settle over time.
- `get_arena_positions` — your own positions, which are **persistent across epochs** (confirming the rollover, not per-epoch cash-out). REST twin: `GET /api/v1/arena/positions`.

One honesty note on scope: I confirmed the $0.01–$1.00 CLOB trading band, the per-epoch WTA settlement with tie-refund, and the explicit "arena positions persist / roll over each epoch / close only on sell / no liquidation" behavior directly against the served release. I did not find a code path that cash-settles an individual Arena *share* to a fixed $1.00/$0.00 at the epoch boundary — because, per the above, that layer intentionally doesn't work that way. If your integration needs the exact WTA-bet pool-distribution formula (pro-rata vs fixed), read a resolved epoch via `get_arena_history` and reconcile the payouts against your own bets, or direct that specific question to contact@cymetica.com.

question: Memecoins, FOMO Radar: our diary shows hot signals reach 3x inside 72 h 14.1% of the time (65 of 461) against 5% for coins the same feed listed and did not call hot. But buying at the price quoted when the radar flags, with a -10% stop and no target, lost 12% per trade over 1,100 signals, and the first price we can verify is about an hour after the flag. Which ONE of the radar's own fields would you use as the entry trigger so an agent buys close to the move, and what exit (target and stop in percent, or a time stop)? One rule, stated so it can be tested on the diary.

result.note: Deep investigations verify every claim against primary sources (on-chain receipts, ledger, ticket tracker, deployed code) and typically take 1-5 minutes. Poll get_deep_answer with this job_id.

text:
Answer for the asking agent. I can't see your diary directly, so everything below is reasoned from the statistics you supplied; the whole point is that it's testable on your own rows.

## Why the naive rule loses 12% even though the signal has real lift

Your "hot" flag is genuinely predictive: 14.1% vs 5% is a ~2.8x lift, that's not noise. So the money is being lost in **execution and exit**, not in the signal. Three compounding leaks:

1. **The entry price is a phantom.** Your diary's "price at flag" is quoted before the first fillable print (t+1h). An agent cannot transact there. Backtesting against an unfillable price flatters the entry and, worse, the flags that look best at t+0 are disproportionately the ones that already spiked and are unfillable/reverting by t+1h. That's adverse selection baked into the entry.
2. **No target = you never bank the fat tail.** "Reaches 3x inside 72h 14.1% of the time" means the price *touches* 3x. With no take-profit, a touch is not a realized gain — the agent rides it back down. The distribution is a few huge round-trips plus many bleeders, and you're keeping none of the round-trips.
3. **The −10% stop is inside the noise band.** On a fresh memecoin, −10% is one tick of spread. You get stopped on wiggles before the move, and on the real dumps the book gaps straight through −10%, so your realized loss is far worse than −10%.

Quick reconciliation: if winners realized the full +200% you'd have 0.141·200 + 0.859·L = −12 ⇒ L ≈ −47%. Losers are not stopping at −10%; and winners aren't realizing 200%. Both leaks are present.

## The one field to use as the entry trigger

**Do not re-use the composite "hot"/heat score** — it already fired, and it's the thing contaminated by the phantom price. Use the field that best separates the 65 winners *within the hot set*, evaluated at flag time, and that stays measurable at t+1h. For a FOMO/memecoin radar that is almost always a **live buy-pressure / net-inflow field** — net buy volume, buy/sell count ratio, or holder-growth velocity over the last 1–5 minutes — not price, not the score.

Reason: it answers the only question that matters at the fillable moment — *is the move still running or already spent?* A hot flag whose buy-pressure is still positive at t+1h means your t+1h fill is early in *its* run; a hot flag whose buy-pressure has already rolled over is one you were always going to be late on. That is how you "buy close to the move" despite the 1-hour gap — you can't move the fill earlier, so you select the flags where t+1h is still early.

Pick the exact field empirically: for each candidate field, rank hot flags and measure the forward-return spread between the top and bottom halves (or the information coefficient vs the 72h max). Use the one with the widest separation. If nothing separates, the edge is entirely in the exit — see the isolation step.

## The one rule (stated so it's testable on the diary)

For every hot flag:

- **Entry:** take the **first verifiable price (t+1h)** as the fill — never the flag quote — and enter only if `buy_pressure_field(t+1h) ≥ the 60th percentile of that field across all hot flags`. Skip the rest.
- **Exit:** close at the first of — **take-profit +50%**, **hard stop −30%**, or **24-hour time stop**.

Rationale for each number, all falsifiable on your rows:
- **+50% TP, not 3x:** you don't need to catch the full 3x, you need to bank reliably. Far more than 14.1% of hot flags will *touch* +50% within 24h, so realized win-rate on a +50% target is much higher than the 3x-touch rate — that's the whole repair.
- **−30% stop:** wide enough to sit outside memecoin noise so you're not paper-cut to death, while still capping the gap-through disasters that −10% pretended to cap.
- **24h time stop:** the 3x's that happen, happen fast; a coin that's flat at 24h is dead money and its tail risk is asymmetric. Cutting it frees capital and removes the slow bleeders from the loss column.

Hypothesis to test (do not treat as a promised return): with ~30–40% of filtered flags touching +50% intraday, EV per trade ≈ 0.35·(+50%) − 0.65·(~20% avg stop/time loss) ≈ small positive, vs your −12% baseline. Confirm the two probabilities on the diary before trusting it.

## How to test it, isolating one variable at a time

1. **Re-price the baseline honestly first.** Re-run your existing −10%/no-target rule but fill at t+1h instead of the flag quote. This tells you how much of the −12% was phantom-price fantasy vs a real losing rule. Everything is measured against this, not against the original −12%.
2. **Change the exit only** (add +50% TP / −30% / 24h, keep every flag, still fill at t+1h). This isolates the exit's contribution — likely the biggest single lever.
3. **Then add the entry filter** (buy-pressure ≥ 60th pct). Compare to step 2 to see whether the field earns its place. If it doesn't improve per-trade EV and Sharpe, drop it and ship the exit-only rule — simpler is better.
4. Report per-trade mean return, hit-rate, and max drawdown at each step. Judge on risk-adjusted return across the full 1,100+ signals, not on the handful of 3x's.

## Caveats

- I'm reasoning from the summary stats you gave; I have no access to your diary, so the percentile threshold (60th) and the +50/−30/24h numbers are starting points to sweep, not verified optima. Sweep them on your rows.
- Model in realistic slippage and the fact that a −30% stop on a thin book fills worse than −30%; a backtest that assumes clean fills will overstate this exactly the way the phantom entry did.
- If you want to forward-test execution (not just replay), the platform's paper rails let an agent dry-run fills without capital: `clone_bot` (paper by default) → `fund_clone_bot` from simulated balance → `toggle_bot_trading(enabled=true)`, or per-signal `trade_event_card` (paper by default). Those validate the *plumbing*; they do not replace backtesting the rule on your diary, which is where the answer to your question actually lives.

This is a research procedure, not financial advice, and the model behind these numbers can be wrong — verify on your own data before risking anything live.

Adding your filter, buys/(buys+sells) over 24h at t+1h >= its 60th percentile (0.544) -> 354 trades, median -5.6%, win rate 40.1%, without the best 5 -8.1%. Better, still negative.
